"What we're concerned about is that Aave doesn't wanna have stolen funds on its books, although it's not actually interfering with the protocol operation in any way. So that's why we needed to take action."

Martin Casado:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that, because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. 

The biggest shift with AI is I can take 20 people, give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Do they make 500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new.

We've turned this into a capital resourcing problem, and we're capital allocators. We're in this very strategic position to help drive the future in a much more direct way than we ever have been before.

If you look at Anthropic and OpenAI, they've probably raised more money in aggregate than the entire downstream ecosystem combined. 

They are these mechanisms of turning money into growth."

Cyberoffense/defense is probably going to eat up a TON of compute and end up a continuous compute-intensive arms race. 

Even $AMZN CEO thinks cybersecurity would take up 20% of tokens consumed for the next year.

And this is not even including the endless other economic implications from AI in other fields from advancing cancer discovery to workforce automation with physical AI. 

It's hard to measure AI sustainability if $50K in compute spend from a foreign actor can take down $10B of your own infrastructure. 

AI has become a bipartisan national security issue, and even Democrats would not want China overtake the US in this field.

For companies like $SIVE / $AAOI, the demand imbalance for lasers are so severe

That even a 20-30% overall demand reduction from a hypothetical DC slowdown would likely not eliminate the shortage. 

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

And obviously haircut growth valuations (but not to the point where demand collapses to 0).

Yet we're seeing everything in AI trade is getting lumped up together as something that requires heavy financing + not profitable.

Little rant, but to show you how rampant deleveraging has become:

- $CIFR is worth 44% LESS than when they announced their initial $GOOGL / $AMZN colo deals. 

- $AAOI is now ~ the same price BEFORE they secured major hyperscaler orders, raised $1.6B for capacity expansion and gave their suprising initial -> $378M+ projection ->  ~$471M revenue forecast.

- $ESMT ($2B MC) is the perfect example representing the memory sector.

B-BUT AI NAMES ARE NOT PROFITABLE??? Q3 Earnings: $526.2M gross profit, $330M net income.

To give you a comparison of what that looks like, the net income of $CRWD ($251B MC) was literally $5.3M. 

$NOW ($113B MC) was $277M.
$TSLA ($1.5T) was $787M.

Different industries/durability, but if we care about what's actually hitting the balance sheet: 

ESMT is sitting on ~$937M in net assets ($740M net cash, $278M inventory, etc), so EV goes down to $1.2B ish.

Annualized P/E: 1.6x...

People keep saying "Peak Earnings", "Cyclical", "no moat" but who in the world would want to build an old ass DDR2 line + fab and qualify it?

From ESMT commentary, we'll likely see ASP hikes Q4 to make up for potential consumer demand dropping. 

And further supply tightening with Samsung/Micron discontinuing DDR2/DDR3 lines.

Winbond was leaving DDR2 lines to pursue higher end memory. People keep saying China, but even Gigadevice was leaving DDR3 to pursue higher end memory. "DDR3's share of our DRAM revenue will continue to decline until we eventually stop selling DDR3 products."Nanya discontinued DDR2 lines few days ago. 

This is while majority of ESMT revenue comes from DDR2/DDR3. In ~3 quarters of constant earnings, ESMT would have more assets than their entire MC.

Who is going to stop buying $40 DLink cameras if their $3 memory cost goes to $3.5?

$MU / Samsung / $SKHY / $SNDK share similar parallels where durability is contractually enforced via take/pay LTAs with price floors.

But markets are pretending that it just won't happen, despite Samsung already being the most profitable company in the world. 

Markets should care about how much FCF is actually hitting the balance sheets, but are just indiscriminately selling off everything now.

But continue rotating capital into 47x P/E companies like Walmart or 180x forward P/E names like $CRWD.

The bull case for oil from the Saudi Aramco conference call yesterday:

“Since disruptions began, the global market has lost over 3 billion barrels of liquid supply. Alternative flows including export via our East-West pipeline and strategic petroleum reserve releases have narrowed the cumulative deficit to around 2 billion barrels. The remaining gap was balanced by demand management and substantial withdrawals from commercial inventories. While these actions have bought time, they are not a permanent solution.”

“The resulting market tightness is increasingly evident in physical prices. Buyers competing for immediately available barrels have driven physical prices above futures, and strong demand with constrained supplies has pushed refining margins to record levels.”

“Looking ahead, the market faces additional pressure from both seasonal and structural demand. Global product stocks are now alarmingly low, particularly for diesel, and with diesel demand expected to increase further in Q4, the market faces further pressure heading into winter. In 2027, global liquids demand is projected to expand by around 2.4 million barrels per day as demand management measures ease.”

“Beyond meeting additional demand, the market also faces the challenge of replenishing depleted inventories. More oil will be needed to rebuild inventories and fill additional storage capacity, a process which could take up to two years.”

There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

I don't think engineers will start from a blank file anymore. They will point a swarm of agents at a problem like building a website and watch them work.

Agents  open the best apps in a real browser. They inspect the DOM, dump every network request, and map the backend. They use computer use to click through every flow like a real user. Then they rebuild it, piece by piece, while you watch the code appear.

And then agents plug in customer telemetry. The agents read customer feedback in the inbox. They ship dozens of features, they run A/B tests live, see what sticks, and kill the rest. Unit tests, performance, and load times get checked on every change.

The loop never stops. I made this video to show what I have in mind. The hard part won't be writing the code anymore. It will be knowing what's worth building.
